Missing the best months, avoiding the worst: why both statistics mislead, and what an actual exit does

Remove the strongest months, the weakest months, or both from an authored decade, then test a real rule: leave after a month-end close and return later. See why large gains and losses tend to arrive together.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test missed strong months, missed weak months and a real exit window

Interactive planning lab

Ending value · out for the 5 best months$12,739.63
Ending value · out for the 5 worst months$27,590.34
Ending value · out for both sets$19,478.68
Ending value · out for months 47–52$15,156.79
Exit window minus fully invested-$2,888.11

An existing $10,000 balance follows one authored 120-month path. Removing a month replaces its return with interest on cash at the entered effective annual rate, converted to a monthly rate. The best and worst months are identified with hindsight, which no investor has in advance. The exit window is a rule a person could actually follow: leave after one month-end close and return after a fixed number of months. No fees, trading costs, tax, spreads or distributions are modeled. The path is a teaching example, not market history, a forecast or a probability.

The central idea

“Missing the best days” and “avoiding the worst days” are hindsight exercises. In volatile stretches the best and worst periods sit side by side, so an exit usually skips some of each. Whether an exit helps depends on dates nobody knows in advance, which is why a written allocation usually serves crash worry better than a forecast.

01

Two famous statistics, and the question neither one answers

Investment articles often show that an investor who missed a handful of the market’s best days ended with far less money than one who stayed invested. A reply soon follows: an investor who missed the worst days would have done far better. Both calculations are correct and both are hindsight. Nobody can list the best or worst periods before they happen.

The useful question is what happens to someone who follows a rule they could actually follow, such as “move to cash after this month-end and come back in six months.” This guide answers both with one authored ten-year path for an existing CAD 10,000 balance. The path is deliberately simple: calm months averaging about 0.5%, a 14-month crisis in months 41 to 54 in which large losses and large gains alternate, then a recovery. Any month spent out of the market earns cash interest, 2.25% a year by default.

02

Remove the best months, the worst months, or both

Fully invested, CAD 10,000 grows to about CAD 18,045. Remove the five best months and it ends at about CAD 12,740. Remove the five worst months and it ends at about CAD 27,590. Remove both sets and it ends at about CAD 19,479, close to staying invested.

The count chart extends this from zero to ten months. Missing more best months keeps lowering the result; missing more worst months keeps raising it. The line for missing both stays within a few thousand dollars of the fully invested balance. Missing both is a closer description of what an imperfect exit does, because of where the months fall.

A practical note: removing a fixed set of months gives the same ending value whatever order the months occur in. Order matters only once a person must choose an exit date, and that is where clustering becomes decisive.

03

The best months are found next to the worst months

In this path the five best months are months 45, 47, 48, 50 and 52; the five worst are 41, 43, 44, 46 and 49. Each best month sits on average about 1.4 months from the nearest worst month. The clustering chart lists them in calendar order.

That arrangement is authored, but it reflects an observation regulators make about real markets. FINRA notes that some of the top trading days occur during periods of greater volatility, so an investor who sells during a sharp but temporary decline may miss the rebound. The months that test nerves and the months that reward patience tend to arrive together.

04

A rule you could follow: leave after a month-end and return later

The default exit leaves after the close of month 46, just after the deepest monthly loss, when fear is likely to be greatest, and stays out for six months. The window skips four strong months and two weak ones. The balance ends at about CAD 15,157, about CAD 2,888 below staying invested.

The heatmap shows fifteen windows. Leaving after month 40, before the trouble starts, and staying out for six months ends about CAD 5,043 ahead, because the window happens to skip the first crash months. Leaving after month 46 for twelve months ends about CAD 4,224 behind. The best cells require knowing that a crisis is about to start; the worst cells follow the natural reaction of selling after large losses and waiting for calm. Choosing the dates required the whole path, which no investor has.

Leaving is also only half of the decision. The exit and re-entry guide shows that the rule for coming back can matter as much as the rule for leaving. Selling a fund in a non-registered account is also a disposition for tax purposes, which this model does not charge.

05

New pay is a separate decision from an existing balance

This guide follows a balance already invested. Money arriving from each paycheque raises a different question: whether to keep investing it on schedule during a volatile period. Regular contributions keep buying through a window like the one above, including some of the low-priced months. Holding new pay in cash until conditions look better turns each deposit into a timing decision; the dip-waiting guide tests that rule, and the cash-floor guide checks whether contributions remain affordable if income stops.

06

Responding to crash worry without forecasting the crash

Worry about a financial-crisis-style fall is reasonable, especially for money needed within a few years. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor education site suggests staying with a diversified portfolio that fits your plan and warns that trying to time the market can mean losses when prices drop and missed gains when they recover. Those points suggest acting on the allocation rather than the calendar:

  • Keep money needed in the next few years outside equities, in cash or short-term savings sized to the expense.
  • Choose an equity share whose loss in a crisis you could hold through; a balanced fund or a mix with bonds lowers the size of a fall but does not prevent one.
  • Write a rebalancing rule in advance; the rebalancing guide shows how one behaves through a crash.
  • Check the costs and tax of any sale before trading in a non-registered account.
  • If a decline would force a change in plans, the risk is too high for the goal, whatever the market does next.

None of these steps promises a recovery by a particular date. Markets have recovered from past declines, but recoveries have taken different lengths of time, and a diversified portfolio can still lose value for years.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. Every monthly return, balance, cash rate and exit window on this page is a hypothetical editable teaching example. The path is not market history, a forecast or a probability, and it is not the record of any index or fund. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FINRA · What Is Market Timing? ↗

    Published 10 June 2025; reviewed 26 October 2026 for top trading days occurring during volatile periods, missed rebounds after selling in a decline, and trading costs and tax. US tax rules are not applied.

  2. OSC GetSmarterAboutMoney · How does market volatility affect your investments? ↗

    Last updated 4 August 2026; reviewed 26 October 2026 for staying with a diversified portfolio, the risks of timing the market and the permanence of selling at low prices.

  3. FINRA · The Benefits and Limitations of Dollar-Cost Averaging ↗

    Published 19 May 2026; reviewed 26 October 2026 for the distinction between money invested as it is earned and cash waiting to be invested.

  4. CRA · Capital Gains – 2025 (T4037) ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 for the disposition of capital property such as mutual fund units. No tax on the exit is calculated in this model.
